title: Aging and Trimming an Animal
dek: Most of what people call gamey was decided before the meat ever saw a kitchen.
activeTime: Several hours across a few days
intro:
Ask ten people why venison tastes strong and you will get ten answers about the animal. Almost always it was the handling. Heat left in the carcass, hair and dirt worked into the meat, fat left on, and silverskin left in place all contribute far more than what the deer was eating. An elk taken care of properly tastes like very good beef with a darker note. One that sat warm in the back of a truck tastes like a mistake.

Aging is a slow, cold, controlled version of the same enzymes that spoil meat when it is warm. Get the temperature right and it tenderises. Get it wrong and you are just growing things.

items: 1 hanging space that holds a steady cold temperature, ideally 34 to 38 degrees Fahrenheit (1 to 3°C)
1 thermometer for that space, checked daily
6 to 10 rolls of butcher paper or a vacuum sealer
2 clean towels for wiping the surface

method: Get the heat out first. Everything else is secondary. A carcass that cools quickly is a carcass you can age; one that does not is one you should be cutting and freezing tonight. Open it up, get air moving through it, and quarter it if that is what it takes.

Hang or hold the meat between 34 and 38 degrees Fahrenheit (1 to 3°C). Above about 40 degrees Fahrenheit (4°C) you are no longer aging, you are spoiling slowly. Below freezing, nothing happens at all. This is a narrow window and a thermometer is not optional.

Judge the time by the animal and the temperature. In that range, a young deer wants three to five days and a mature elk five to ten. There is no gain past about two weeks on a home setup, and there is real risk.

Expect the outside to dry into a dark, firm crust. That is normal and it gets trimmed away. What is not normal is anything slimy, anything green, or any sour smell that persists after you have wiped the surface. Trust your nose. It is a better instrument than any rule of thumb.

If you cannot hold that temperature, do not age. Quarter the animal, bone it out and get it cold or frozen. Coolers with ice, drained daily so the meat is not sitting in water, will hold quarters for several days and are how most people here manage it.

When you break it down, remove every scrap of fat. Deer and elk fat is waxy, it does not render pleasantly, it coats the roof of your mouth, and it goes rancid in the freezer faster than anything else on the animal. This is the single biggest flavour decision you will make.

Take out any blood-shot meat, any hair that has worked into the surface, and anything that smells of gut. Cut wide around it. The instinct to save every ounce is exactly how one bad spot flavours twenty pounds of burger.

Separate the muscles at their seams rather than sawing across them. Push a thumb into the natural line between two muscles and they come apart cleanly, which gives you whole pieces to cook rather than a pile of odd chunks.
Sort as you go into three piles: steaks and roasts, braising cuts, and grind. Shanks, neck and anything laced with connective tissue go to braise or grind, never to a hot pan.
Wrap tightly and label. Air is the enemy in a freezer, and a package you cannot identify in the dark is a package that gets used last, if ever.

On disease and parasites: freezing does not make everything safe and it does not substitute for testing. Rules and recommendations around chronic wasting disease, sampling, and what to do with an animal that looked wrong are Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife's to publish, and they change. Check with ODFW and your state's current hunter guide rather than taking a recipe page's word for any of it.
notes: A dedicated old refrigerator with the shelves pulled out and a small fan inside is the most practical aging chamber most households will ever have.
Bone-in aging protects the meat from drying but takes more space. Boned-out muscles age faster and need watching.
storage: Wrapped tight and held at 0 degrees Fahrenheit (-18°C), whole-muscle cuts keep their quality about a year and ground meat about four months. Both are safe indefinitely at that temperature; it is quality that degrades, not safety.

title: Getting the Silverskin Off
dek: The livery taste people blame on the deer is usually still attached to the meat.
intro:
Silverskin is the pearly sheet of connective tissue that wraps whole muscles. It is not fat, it does not render, and it does not soften with cooking. Under heat it shrinks harder than the meat does, which curls a steak into a bowl and squeezes it tight, and it carries a strong metallic flavour that people confuse with the animal itself.

Removing it properly takes a thin flexible knife and about twenty minutes of patience. It is the highest-return knife skill in this whole category, and it is worth doing badly a few times to learn.

items: 1 boning or fillet knife, thin, flexible, genuinely sharp
1 large cutting board with a damp towel under it
1 venison or elk backstrap, roast or whole muscle, chilled

method: Work with cold meat. Cold muscle is firm and holds its shape under a knife; room temperature muscle is soft and slippery and you will take meat off with the skin.

Find an edge of the silverskin at the thick end and slide the knife tip underneath to lift a flap about an inch wide. Get enough of a tab that you can hold it firmly with a paper towel between your fingers and the meat.
Angle the blade slightly upward, into the silverskin rather than into the meat. This is the whole trick, and it feels wrong the first three times you do it.
Pull the tab taut with your free hand and push the knife forward in a shallow sawing motion, keeping tension the entire time. The skin peels off in a strip and the blade rides along underneath it.
Do not try to take it all in one piece. Two or three strips down the length of a backstrap is normal and faster than fighting for a single sheet.

Check the result by running a palm over the muscle. It should feel like bare meat, faintly tacky, with no smooth slick patches. Any silver you can still see will still be there when it comes off the grill.
Turn the muscle over and repeat on any seams and on the strip of tough tissue that runs down the underside of a backstrap.
Trim any remaining fat while you are here. On deer and elk it is waxy, it does not improve anything, and it is where rancid freezer flavours start.

A cleaned muscle also cooks more predictably, which matters because whole-muscle venison is pulled at an internal temperature of 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit (54 to 57°C) and a curled, unevenly thick piece will not read honestly on a probe.

Keep the trimmings separate. Meat scraped off the silverskin goes in the grind pile; the skin itself goes in the bin, or into a stockpot if you want gelatin, where long wet heat will finally break it down.

What goes wrong: cutting downward. If your strips are coming off with a layer of red meat attached, raise the back of the knife and let the blade climb toward the surface. You want a translucent ribbon, not a steak.
notes: A dull knife makes this nearly impossible. Sharpen before you start, not halfway through when you are annoyed.
Nobody gets a clean backstrap on the first animal. It is a physical skill and it arrives after about the fourth one.
storage: Cleaned whole muscles wrap tighter and freeze better than untrimmed ones, because there is less surface irregularity to trap air. Vacuum seal if you can, double wrap if you cannot.

title: Venison Backstrap, Reverse Seared
dek: The best cut on the animal, and the easiest one to ruin in ninety seconds.
intro:
Backstrap is the loin that runs along the outside of the spine, and it is lean enough that the usual hot-pan-then-rest routine leaves a grey band an eighth of an inch thick around a raw middle. Reverse searing fixes that: a low oven brings the whole piece up gently and evenly, and then a very short violent sear builds the crust at the end, when there is no time left to overcook anything.

Whole-muscle venison and elk take the same latitude as a beef steak. Ground is a different matter entirely, but an intact steak from a healthy animal is treated exactly like beef, medium rare and all.

items: 1 venison backstrap section, about 1.5 lb (680 g), silverskin removed
1 tbsp beef tallow or neutral oil

method: Salt the backstrap on all sides and let it sit on a rack, uncovered, in the fridge for at least an hour and up to overnight. Salt needs time to move inward, and the dry surface it leaves behind is what lets you build a crust in one minute later.
Heat the oven to 250°F (120°C) and set the meat on a rack over a sheet pan, still uncovered. Pepper it now.

Roast slowly until a probe in the centre reads about 115 to 118 degrees Fahrenheit (46 to 48°C). The outside will look pale and unappetising and the meat will feel springy rather than soft. Expect 35 to 50 minutes depending on thickness, and go by the probe.
Rest it on the counter while you get a heavy skillet ripping hot with the tallow, to the point where it shimmers and the first smoke lifts. Anything less and the sear takes too long.

Sear the backstrap on every side, turning every 30 seconds or so, until the entire surface is deeply browned and crusted. This should take about two minutes total. Use tongs and stand it on its edges as well.
Add butter, thyme, garlic and juniper in the last thirty seconds, tilt the pan, and spoon the foaming butter over the meat. Then get it out.

Pull at an internal temperature of 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit (54 to 57°C) for medium rare, which is the same target you would use for a whole-muscle beef steak and the point at which the meat is deep pink through with a thin brown band at the edge. Rest 10 minutes.

For the sauce, pour off most of the fat, cook the shallot until translucent, deglaze with the wine and reduce it until the pan is nearly dry and the smell has turned from sharp to sweet. Add stock, reduce by half, then swirl in cold butter and the vinegar off the heat.
Slice across the grain, about half an inch thick, and pour the sauce over.

What goes wrong: cooking it to well done out of nerves about wild game. That turns the leanest cut on the animal into sawdust. If you want reassurance, the internal temperature guidance for whole-muscle game is the same as for whole-muscle beef; the higher figure of 160°F (71°C) applies to ground meat, where surface bacteria get mixed throughout.
notes: Tenderloins, which sit inside the body cavity, are smaller and even leaner. Same method, half the oven time, watch them closely.
If the animal was not handled well in the field, no cooking method rescues the backstrap. Cook that one as stew and take better care of the next one.
storage: Cooked backstrap keeps three days and is best eaten cold and sliced thin rather than reheated. Raw, vacuum sealed, it holds a year at 0 degrees Fahrenheit (-18°C) without meaningful loss.

title: Elk Steak in a Cast Iron Pan
dek: Beefier than beef, half the fat, and the pan needs to be hotter than you think.
intro:
Elk is the most beef-like of the wild meats and the easiest sell to somebody who claims not to like game. It is also leaner than any beef you can buy, which means the fat that normally lubricates a steak and buys you thirty seconds of margin is simply not present.

So the fat comes from the pan. A hard sear in tallow, a butter baste at the end, and a resting plate with more butter on it. The other adjustment is thickness: cut elk steaks thicker than you would cut beef, because a thin lean steak is overcooked before it is browned.

items: 4 elk steaks from the round or sirloin, 1.25 inches thick, about 8 oz (225 g) each
2 tbsp beef tallow or clarified butter
2 tbsp softened butter mashed with 1 tsp chopped rosemary

method: Salt the steaks on both sides and leave them on a rack in the fridge, uncovered, for 45 minutes. This dries the surface and seasons the inside, and both matter more on lean meat than on marbled beef.
Take them out and let them lose the worst of the chill while the pan heats. A cold steak in a hot pan cooks its outside twice as far before the middle wakes up.
Heat a cast iron skillet over high heat, dry, until a drop of water bounces and skitters instead of sitting and boiling. That takes several minutes and there is no shortcut.

Add the tallow, swirl once, and lay the steaks in without crowding. Two at a time in a ten inch pan. You should hear a hard continuous sizzle immediately; if you hear a polite one, the pan was not ready.
Leave them alone until a proper crust has formed and the steak releases from the pan without tearing, about two to three minutes. Then flip once.

Drop in butter, rosemary and garlic, tilt the pan and baste continuously with a spoon. The butter should be foaming and smell nutty, not black and acrid; pull the pan off the heat for a moment if it is getting away from you.

Pull the steaks at an internal temperature of 125 to 130 degrees Fahrenheit (52 to 54°C), because they will climb five degrees while resting to land at medium rare. Whole-muscle elk gets the same treatment as a whole-muscle beef steak; the 160°F (71°C) rule is for ground meat only.
Rest on a warm plate with the rosemary butter melting on top, at least 8 minutes. Skipping the rest costs you the juice on the board instead of in the meat.
Slice across the grain and finish with flaky salt and lemon zest.

What goes wrong: medium well. Elk past about 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63°C) goes dry, grainy and slightly liver-ish, and it does it fast. If your household insists on well done, cook that portion as a braise instead and everyone will be happier.
notes: Round steaks from an older animal benefit from a light jaccard or a fork stab all over before salting. Sirloin does not need it.
Cast iron holds heat; thin stainless does not. If a lightweight pan is all you have, do two steaks at a time and let it recover between batches.
storage: Raw steaks keep three days in the fridge, a year vacuum sealed in the freezer at 0 degrees Fahrenheit (-18°C). Cooked, three days, and sliced cold into a sandwich they are better than reheated.

title: Slow-Braised Shoulder
dek: The cut nobody wants, cooked the only way it was ever going to work.
intro:
A shoulder is a working muscle group laced with connective tissue, and every attempt to treat it like a steak ends the same way. Under long wet heat, though, that same connective tissue turns to gelatin, and gelatin is what makes a braise feel rich even though there is almost no fat in the animal.

The requirement is time at a low temperature. A braise held at a hard boil tightens the muscle fibres and squeezes them dry, so you end up with stringy meat sitting in good sauce. Barely a bubble, lid on, several hours, and do not go poking at it.

items: 4 lb (1.8 kg) venison or elk shoulder, boned, in large chunks
3 tbsp beef tallow or neutral oil

method: Trim the shoulder hard. Every bit of waxy fat and every sheet of silverskin you leave will float to the top of the braise as a greasy film and taste of the freezer. Connective tissue between muscles can stay; that is the good kind.
Season the chunks, dust them with flour, and shake off the excess. Heat the tallow in a heavy Dutch oven until it shimmers.

Brown the meat in batches, without crowding, until each piece has a genuinely dark crust on at least two sides and the bottom of the pot has gone brown and sticky. Pale meat gives a pale braise; this step is the flavour.

Set the meat aside, lower the heat, and cook the onions, carrots and celery in the fat until softened and browning at the edges. Add garlic and tomato paste and cook, stirring, until the paste darkens from red to brick and smells sweet rather than tinny.
Pour in the wine and scrape everything off the bottom with a wooden spoon. Reduce it by half, which takes the raw edge off and concentrates it.
Return the meat, add stock to come about three quarters of the way up, then the thyme, bay, juniper and orange peel. Bring it just to a simmer on the stove.

Cover and move it to a 300°F (150°C) oven. Check after 30 minutes: the liquid should be barely trembling, with a bubble breaking every second or two. If it is bubbling steadily, drop the oven by 25 degrees Fahrenheit.

Cook until a fork pushed into a chunk twists freely with no resistance and the meat begins to fall apart at the seams under its own weight. That is roughly three and a half to four and a half hours, and it is a texture, not a time.

Braising takes the meat far past any internal temperature target, which is the point; connective tissue only converts to gelatin somewhere above 160°F (71°C) and it needs hours there. Doneness here is texture, not a number on a probe.

Lift the meat out, strain the liquid, and skim the fat off the top. Reduce the strained liquid hard on the stove until it coats a spoon and leaves a clear line when you drag a finger across the back of it.
Off the heat, swirl in the cold butter and the vinegar. The vinegar is not optional; it cuts the richness and makes the whole pot taste like it has seasoning rather than just salt.
Return the meat to the sauce, warm it through, and scatter parsley over. Serve on mashed potatoes, polenta or noodles.
What goes wrong: a boil. If the meat comes out stringy and dry inside a great sauce, the pot was too hot. Same recipe, lower oven, next time.
notes: Better the second day, genuinely. The gelatin sets overnight and the fat lifts off the top in a solid disc, which is the easiest skimming you will ever do.
Neck meat is the same proposition as shoulder and often better. Do not grind either of them if you have the time to braise.
storage: Fridge four days, freezer three months in its sauce. Freeze the meat submerged in liquid or the exposed edges dry out and go woolly.

title: Shanks, Osso Buco Style
dek: Cross-cut shanks, a long slow oven, and the marrow is the reason.
intro:
Most people grind shanks, which is a waste of the most interesting cut on a deer or an elk. A shank is dense muscle wrapped around a bone full of marrow, and it is nearly all connective tissue, which under a long braise becomes something no other cut can produce. Ask a butcher to cross-cut them into thick rounds, or do it yourself with a bone saw.

The gremolata at the end is not a garnish. Raw lemon zest, garlic and parsley scattered over a heavy braise is the thing that keeps four hours of rich cooking from being monotonous by the third bite.

items: 6 cross-cut venison or elk shanks, about 2 inches thick
1 can whole tomatoes, 28 oz (800 g), crushed by hand

method: Tie a length of twine around the circumference of each shank. They will fall apart in the pot otherwise, and half the pleasure is putting a whole round on a plate with the bone standing up in the middle.
Season the shanks, dredge them in flour, and knock off the excess. Heat the oil in a wide Dutch oven over medium-high.

Brown them thoroughly on both flat faces, in batches, until a hard mahogany crust has formed and they lift away from the pan without sticking. This takes longer than you want it to; do not rush it and do not crowd the pan.
Remove the shanks. Lower the heat and cook the onion, carrot and celery in the same fat until soft, sweet-smelling and just starting to catch at the edges of the pot.
Add garlic and tomato paste, stirring until the paste turns brick red and smells cooked rather than sharp. Deglaze with the white wine, scraping the bottom clean, and let it reduce by half.
Add tomatoes, stock, thyme, bay and lemon peel. Settle the shanks back in so the liquid comes about two thirds of the way up but does not cover them; the exposed tops brown while the bottoms braise.
Bring to a bare simmer on the stove, cover, and put it in a 300°F (150°C) oven. Peek after half an hour to confirm the liquid is barely moving. Anything more vigorous will string the meat out.

Braise until the meat has pulled back from the bone, a fork twists in it with no resistance, and the marrow in the centre has gone soft and glossy. Figure three and a half to four hours, and check rather than trusting the clock.

There is no useful internal temperature target for a shank. It goes well past 160°F (71°C) within the first hour and then spends three more hours converting connective tissue, so you judge it with a fork and not a thermometer.
Lift the shanks out carefully and snip off the twine. Skim the fat from the sauce and, if it is thin, reduce it on the stovetop until it coats a spoon.
Chop the gremolata ingredients together on a board so the oils mix, and scatter over each shank at the table. Serve with polenta, risotto or bread.
What goes wrong: shanks submerged completely and cooked hot. They come out grey and shredded. Half-submerged and barely simmering is the whole method.
notes: A marrow spoon or the handle of a teaspoon is the correct tool for the middle of the bone. Whoever cooked it gets first go.
This is a good candidate for making a day ahead. Cool it in the pot, refrigerate, lift the fat off, and reheat gently in the oven.
storage: Fridge four days in the sauce, freezer three months. Reheat covered at 300°F (150°C) until the sauce is bubbling gently at the edges and the meat is hot through.

title: Venison Stew for a Wet Week
dek: Dark, thick, and better on the third day than it was on the first.
intro:
Stew is where the awkward parts of the animal go: the front quarter, the neck, the bits that came off the bone in shapes nobody wants to look at on a plate. Cut into cubes and braised for hours, all of it becomes the same good thing.

The two decisions that separate a great pot from a grey one are browning the meat properly and keeping the pot below a simmer once the lid is on. Everything else is a matter of what is in the vegetable drawer, and stew has never been a recipe so much as a method with suggestions attached.

items: 3 lb (1.4 kg) venison stew meat, in 1.5 inch cubes, silverskin removed
4 tbsp beef tallow or neutral oil
1.5 cups red wine or dark beer
1.5 lb (680 g) waxy potatoes, in chunks

method: Render the bacon in a heavy pot until crisp, lift it out, and leave the fat. Season the venison cubes and toss them in flour, shaking off what does not cling.

Brown the meat in batches in the bacon fat and tallow, giving each batch room and leaving it undisturbed until a dark crust forms and it releases on its own. A crowded pot steams, and steamed meat makes grey stew.
Set the meat aside. Cook the onions in the fat until they are soft and picking up colour, then add garlic and tomato paste and stir until the paste darkens and smells sweet.
Deglaze with the wine, scraping every brown speck off the bottom, and reduce it by half.

Return the meat and bacon, add stock, Worcestershire, thyme, bay and paprika. Bring it to a bare simmer, cover, and hold it there over the lowest heat that keeps a bubble breaking every couple of seconds.

After about two hours, test a cube. It should be tender enough to crush against the roof of your mouth but still holding together. If it squeaks or resists, it needs longer, and no amount of stirring will hurry it.
Add potatoes, carrots and parsnips and cook until they are tender to a knife tip with no chalky centre, roughly 30 minutes. Adding them at the start turns them to paste.
Brown the mushrooms separately in a dry hot pan until they have given up their water and squeaked, then browned, and stir them in. Mushrooms added raw to a stew just release water and dilute it.
Stir in the peas at the very end and let them heat through for two minutes so they stay green. Taste for salt, add the parsley, and let the pot sit off the heat for 15 minutes before serving.

What goes wrong: thin stew. If it is watery, lift the meat and vegetables out and reduce the liquid hard until it coats a spoon, then put everything back. Do not add flour at the end; it tastes raw and never quite disappears.
notes: Any whole-muscle game works. The internal temperature rules that matter for ground meat do not apply here, because a long braise takes everything far past any of them.
A square of dark chocolate or a spoon of instant coffee stirred in at the end deepens the colour and the flavour without tasting of either.
storage: Fridge five days, and it improves for the first three. Freezes three months, though the potatoes go slightly grainy; leave them out if you are freezing it deliberately.

title: Ground Venison Chili
dek: Ground game gets cooked to a number, and this is where that number matters.
intro:
Ground meat is a different food safety proposition from a steak. Grinding takes whatever was on the outside surfaces and distributes it through the whole batch, so there is no intact interior to rely on. That is why ground venison, elk, beef and everything else gets cooked to 160°F (71°C) all the way through, and why the medium-rare latitude a backstrap enjoys does not transfer.

Chili takes that requirement in stride, since it simmers for hours anyway. What it needs from you is a real browning at the start and toasted whole spices, which is the difference between chili and meat in red sauce.

items: 8 oz (225 g) bacon or pork fat, diced
4 dried ancho chiles, stemmed and seeded
2 dried guajillo chiles, stemmed and seeded
2 cans kidney or pinto beans, 15 oz (425 g) each, drained
2 tbsp masa harina mixed with 1/4 cup water

method: Toast the dried chiles in a dry skillet over medium heat, pressing them flat, until they smell nutty and turn pliable, about 30 seconds a side. Do not let them blacken; burnt chile is bitter and there is no fixing it.

Cover them with the boiling water and soak until soft, then blend with a cup of the soaking liquid into a smooth paste. This is the actual chili flavour, and it is why the powdered jar version tastes flat.
Render the bacon or pork fat in a heavy pot until the fat has run out. Ground venison has almost no fat of its own, and without added fat it browns into dry pellets.

Brown the venison in batches over high heat, pressing it flat and leaving it to crust before breaking it up. Cooked properly it goes deep brown with crisp edges; stirred constantly it just turns grey and weeps water.

Confirm the meat has reached an internal temperature of 160°F (71°C) with a probe pushed into the thickest part of the layer. Ground meat of any species gets that number and there is no medium-rare version of this dish.
Add onions to the pot and cook until soft, then garlic, cumin, paprika, oregano and coriander, stirring until the spices smell toasted and start to stick.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook it until it darkens, then add the chile paste, the beer, tomatoes and stock. Scrape the bottom clean.
Simmer uncovered, at a lazy bubble, until the chili has darkened, thickened, and a spoon dragged across the bottom leaves a trail that fills in slowly. That is roughly an hour and a half.
Add the beans and cook 20 minutes more so they take on flavour. Stir in the masa slurry and simmer until it thickens and the raw corn flavour has cooked out, about 10 minutes.
Finish with the vinegar off the heat, taste for salt, and let it sit half an hour before serving. Chili served the minute it stops cooking always tastes unfinished.
notes: Ground venison at the butcher is often already mixed with pork or beef fat. If yours is straight venison, the added fat here is doing necessary work, not enriching for the sake of it.
Chunked venison instead of ground makes a coarser and arguably better chili. It also then follows braising rules, not ground-meat rules.
storage: Fridge five days, freezer four months. It thickens on standing, so loosen with stock rather than water when reheating.

title: Venison Burgers, With the Fat Put Back
dek: A wild animal has no fat worth eating, so you supply it or you eat a hockey puck.
intro:
Straight ground venison makes a burger that is dry, crumbly and slightly liver-ish, and no amount of egg or breadcrumb fixes it. The problem is arithmetic: a good beef burger runs somewhere around twenty percent fat, and a deer is closer to two. What you add back matters as much as how much.

Beef fat is the safe answer and pork fat is the better-tasting one. Deer and elk fat is the wrong answer, because it is waxy, it does not render, and it coats your mouth. Trim it off and buy something else to put in.

items: 2 lb (900 g) venison, trimmed of all fat and silverskin, in cubes
8 oz (225 g) beef fat trim or pork back fat, in cubes
2 tbsp beef tallow or neutral oil

method: Put the meat, the fat, the grinder parts and a bowl in the freezer for 30 minutes. Everything should be firm and near freezing but not solid. Warm fat smears instead of cutting, and smeared fat renders straight out in the pan and leaves you back where you started.

Grind the venison and fat together once through a coarse plate, mixed roughly so the ratio stays even. Twenty percent fat by weight is the target, which is where the eight ounces to two pounds comes from.

Season the ground meat with salt, pepper and the powders and mix with two forks, lightly and briefly. Working ground meat hard develops the proteins into a springy, sausage-like texture that eats wrong in a burger.

Form six loose patties slightly wider than the buns and press a shallow dimple into the centre of each with your thumb. Patties swell in the middle as they cook; the dimple is what stops them turning into domes.
Chill the patties 20 minutes. Cold patties hold their shape and let you build a crust before the middle catches up.

Heat a cast iron skillet or a griddle over medium-high with the tallow until it shimmers and a drop of water skitters. Butter and toast the buns first, until the cut faces are golden, and set them aside.

Cook the patties without moving them until the underside has a solid brown crust and the edges look cooked a third of the way up, then flip once. Add cheese after the flip and cover the pan for a minute so it melts.

Cook ground venison to an internal temperature of 160°F (71°C), checked with a probe pushed in from the side of the patty. This is not the place for medium rare. Grinding spreads whatever was on the outside of the meat all through the batch, which is the whole reason ground meat has a higher target than a steak does.
Rest the patties two minutes on a warm plate while you dress the buns. Building straight out of the pan means the juice runs into the bottom bun and it collapses.
What goes wrong: overworking the mix and pressing the patties in the pan. Pressing squeezes out the fat you deliberately added, which is an expensive way to make a dry burger.
notes: Bacon ends work as the added fat and bring salt and smoke with them. Reduce the added salt if you go that way.
If you have the grinder out, do a double batch and freeze the patties between squares of parchment. They cook from frozen over lower heat with a lid on.
storage: Raw patties keep two days in the fridge and three months in the freezer, wrapped tight. Ground game generally holds its quality about four months at 0 degrees Fahrenheit (-18°C), less than whole muscle, because there is far more cut surface exposed.

title: Venison Breakfast Sausage
dek: Sage, pork fat, a cold grind and a test patty before you commit twelve pounds.
intro:
Breakfast sausage is the most forgiving thing you can do with a lot of venison trim, and it is the fastest route to a household that eats what you brought home. It is fresh sausage, meaning no cure and no nitrite: it is a raw ground meat product that gets cooked and eaten like one, not a preserved thing.

The two rules are cold and the test patty. Everything stays near freezing so the fat cuts cleanly rather than smearing, and you fry a spoonful before you shape five pounds, because seasoning ground meat is impossible to judge raw.

items: 3.5 lb (1.6 kg) venison trim, all silverskin and fat removed, in cubes
1.5 lb (680 g) pork shoulder or pork back fat, in cubes

method: Cube the meat and fat and spread it on trays in the freezer for 30 to 45 minutes, until the edges are crunchy but the middles still give. Chill the grinder head, auger, blade and plate at the same time.
Toss the cold cubes with all the dry seasoning so it is distributed before grinding rather than mixed in afterwards, which is more even and less handling.

Grind everything once through a coarse plate into a chilled bowl set over ice. If the meat starts coming out as a smear rather than distinct strands, stop, put everything back in the freezer for fifteen minutes, and start again.
For a finer texture, run half of it through a second time on a smaller plate. Keep the other half coarse, which gives the finished sausage some structure.

Add the ice water and mix with a paddle or your hands for about a minute, until the mixture turns slightly sticky and a handful holds together when you open your palm. That tackiness is the protein binding; it is what stops the patties crumbling.

Fry a small test patty in a skillet until browned on both sides and cooked through, then taste it. Adjust salt, sage and heat now. Raw sausage always tastes under-seasoned, so trust the cooked patty and nothing else.
Rest the mix, covered, in the fridge overnight. The salt and spices need time to move through, and sausage eaten the same day tastes like meat with sage on it rather than sausage.
Shape into patties or stuff into hog casings. For patties, weigh them so they cook at the same rate, and stack them with parchment between.

To cook, start in a cold or barely warm skillet over medium heat rather than a hot one. Lean sausage seizes and dries in a screaming pan. Cook until deeply browned on both faces and the juices run clear.
Cook to an internal temperature of 160°F (71°C) all the way through, checked with a probe in the thickest patty. This is a fresh ground pork and venison product and that number is not negotiable.
What goes wrong: warm grinding. Smeared fat gives a sausage that renders out into a greasy pan and leaves a dry, crumbly patty behind. Cold, cold, cold.
notes: Maple version: swap the brown sugar for 3 tbsp real maple syrup and add it with the ice water.
This is a fresh sausage. It contains no curing salt and it is not shelf stable, smoked or otherwise preserved. Treat it exactly as you would raw ground pork.
storage: Fridge two days raw, three months in the freezer wrapped tight. Cooked patties keep four days and reheat well in a covered skillet with a spoon of water.

title: Summer Sausage, and a Word About Nitrite
dek: A cured, smoked, shelf-friendly sausage where the curing salt is a safety ingredient, not a flavour one.
totalTime: 2 days including the cure and the smoke
intro:
Summer sausage is a cured sausage held for hours at low temperatures in a smoker, which is precisely the temperature range where Clostridium botulinum is happiest. Curing salt containing sodium nitrite is what makes that process safe, and it is not an optional flavouring you can leave out because you would rather not use it. Leave it out and you are making something else, and something riskier.

It is also toxic in excess, which is why it is dyed pink so nobody confuses it with table salt, and why the ratio below comes from tested guidance rather than from anybody's judgement. Weigh it on a scale that reads grams. Do not scoop it.

items: 3.5 lb (1.6 kg) venison, trimmed clean, in cubes
1.5 lb (680 g) pork shoulder or pork fat, in cubes

ingredients.group: Cure and seasoning, for 5 lb of meat
items: 1 level tsp Prague Powder No. 1, which is 6.25 percent sodium nitrite, weighed at about 5.7 g
1 gram scale that reads to a tenth of a gram
1 probe thermometer with a long lead

method: Read a tested recipe before you start, and use its cure ratio rather than this page's if they differ. The standard guidance for Prague Powder No. 1 is one level teaspoon per five pounds of meat, and both halves of that sentence matter: the right product, and the right weight for the batch you actually have.

Understand what the nitrite is for. It inhibits Clostridium botulinum during the long warm smoke, it keeps the meat pink, and it contributes the tang people associate with the style. It is a preservative doing a safety job in a process specifically designed around it.
Chill everything: meat, fat, grinder parts, bowls. Grind the venison and pork together once through a coarse plate, then run half through a fine plate for a tighter texture.
Weigh the cure on the gram scale and dissolve it in the ice water along with the salt, so it disperses evenly instead of sitting in pockets. Uneven cure is both a safety problem and a taste problem.

Add the cure water and the rest of the seasoning to the meat and mix hard for two to three minutes, until the mix is sticky enough that a handful sticks to an upturned palm. That bind is what gives summer sausage its sliceable texture.
Cover and refrigerate 24 hours. The cure needs that time to distribute all the way through, and you cannot shorten it by mixing longer.
Stuff into soaked fibrous casings firmly, without air pockets, and tie the ends. Prick any bubbles you can see. Air pockets are where things go wrong.

Bring the smoker up slowly. Start dry around 130 degrees Fahrenheit (54°C) for an hour with no smoke to dry the casing, then add smoke and step the chamber up by roughly 10 degrees Fahrenheit every hour to a maximum of 175°F (80°C).

Cook until the internal temperature of the chubs reaches 155 to 160°F (68 to 71°C). Use a probe in the centre of the thickest chub and leave it there. Pushing the chamber hot to hurry this renders the fat out and leaves greasy pockets under the casing.

Plunge the finished chubs into an ice water bath until the internal temperature drops below about 110 degrees Fahrenheit (43°C). This stops the cooking, sets the texture, and gets the sausage down through the warm range quickly.
Bloom them at room temperature for an hour, then refrigerate overnight before slicing. Cutting into a warm chub gives you a crumbly face and a disappointment.

If any of this feels like guesswork, stop and find a tested recipe with stated weights from a source that publishes them properly. Cured sausage is not a place for improvisation, and nobody at this store has cooked this particular batch for you.
notes: Prague Powder No. 1 is for anything cooked. Prague Powder No. 2 contains nitrate as well and is for long dry-cured products that are never cooked. They are not interchangeable.
Keep curing salt labelled, in its own container, well away from the salt cellar. It is dyed pink for exactly this reason.
storage: Refrigerated, wrapped, about three weeks. Vacuum sealed and frozen, six months. Despite the name, treat it as a refrigerated product rather than something to leave in a cupboard.

title: Venison Jerky With the Safety Step
dek: Drying alone does not make meat safe, which is the part most jerky recipes skip.
intro:
Jerky is dried meat, and the mistake in most home recipes is assuming drying is the same as cooking. It is not. A dehydrator running at a typical setting removes water slowly enough that bacteria can adapt and survive the process, and dried survivors are still there when you eat it three weeks later.

The fix is one extra step, recommended by USDA and Extension services: bring the meat to an internal temperature of 160°F (71°C) either before drying or right after. That is the whole difference between jerky and a gamble, and it costs you fifteen minutes.

items: 3 lb (1.4 kg) venison from the round or another lean roast, all fat and silverskin removed
1 dehydrator or an oven that will hold 175°F (80°C)
4 wire racks and sheet pans if using the oven

method: Freeze the roast for about an hour until it is firm at the edges. Partly frozen meat slices evenly, and even slices are the difference between a batch that finishes together and one that has burnt strips and damp ones in the same tray.
Trim every trace of fat. Fat does not dry, it goes rancid, and it is the reason a batch of jerky tastes wrong after two weeks in a jar.
Slice a quarter inch thick. With the grain gives chewy jerky, across the grain gives tender jerky that breaks apart more easily. Pick one and be consistent within the batch.
Whisk the marinade and submerge the strips, pressing out the air. Refrigerate 6 to 24 hours. Longer is saltier, not better, and past a day the texture starts to go mushy.

Now the safety step. The straightforward version: lay the drained strips on racks over sheet pans and put them in an oven at 275°F (135°C) until a probe pushed lengthwise into a thick strip reads an internal temperature of 160°F (71°C). That usually takes about ten to fifteen minutes and the meat will look cooked and grey rather than dried.

Alternatively, dry first and heat afterwards, which some people prefer for texture: dry to finished, then hold the strips in a 275°F (135°C) oven for ten minutes to reach the same internal temperature. Either order works; skipping it entirely does not.
Move the strips to the dehydrator at 160 to 165°F (71 to 74°C), or to an oven at its lowest setting with the door propped open a crack and a fan nearby. Leave space between strips so air can move.

Dry until a strip bends and cracks along the bend but does not snap in half, and shows no wet or shiny spots when you tear one open. That is typically four to six hours, and thickness matters more than the clock.
Cool the strips completely on the racks before packing. Warm jerky in a sealed bag sweats, and that condensation is exactly what you spent six hours removing.
Condition it: pack loosely in a jar for a day and shake it occasionally. If you see any condensation on the glass, it needs more drying time. If you see mould at any point, the whole batch goes out.

A note on wild game specifically. Freezing does not reliably kill everything, and this style of drying is not a substitute for cooking. For anything to do with parasites, chronic wasting disease sampling or testing an animal that looked unwell, go to the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife and your current state hunter guide rather than a recipe.
notes: Ground meat jerky pressed through a jerky gun follows the same rule and is less forgiving, because there is no intact interior at all. The heat step matters more there, not less.
A dehydrator that will not hold at least 160°F (71°C) is fine, provided you are doing the oven heat step. Do not use one as your only heat source.
storage: In a sealed jar in a cool cupboard, two to three weeks. In the fridge, two months. In the freezer, a year. Oxygen absorbers help; a scrap of moisture does not.

title: A Venison Roast That Is Not Dry
dek: A lean roast wants a low oven, a probe, and someone willing to take it out early.
intro:
A whole-muscle roast off the hind quarter, the top round or the sirloin tip, is one of the best things on a deer and one of the most commonly ruined. It has no marbling and no fat cap, so there is nothing basting it from inside, and the difference between rosy and grey is about fifteen minutes in a conventional oven.

A low oven narrows that gap by cooking the whole roast at nearly the same rate rather than in layers. Add a fat cap you supply yourself, a probe left in the meat, and a proper rest, and it behaves.

items: 1 venison or elk roast, 3 to 4 lb (1.4 to 1.8 kg), silverskin removed, tied
6 slices bacon or a sheet of pork back fat

method: Salt the roast all over and leave it uncovered on a rack in the fridge overnight if you can, or at least two hours. Dry brining seasons the interior and dries the surface so it browns.
Tie the roast into an even cylinder with twine at inch intervals. An untied roast has a thin flapping end that is grey before the middle is warm.
Heat the oven to 250°F (120°C). Smear the roast with mustard, garlic and herbs, then drape the bacon or fat over the top and tie it in place.
Scatter onions and carrots in a roasting pan, set the roast on top, and push a probe into the very centre along the long axis.

Roast slowly. On a roast this size in a low oven, expect somewhere between an hour and a half and two hours, but the probe is the only thing that decides. The exterior will look pale for most of that time and that is correct.

Pull the roast at an internal temperature of 125 to 128 degrees Fahrenheit (52 to 53°C) if you want medium rare after carryover, or 135 degrees Fahrenheit (57°C) for medium. Whole-muscle venison and elk take the same latitude as whole-muscle beef; only ground meat needs 160°F (71°C).
Rest the roast, loosely tented, for a full 20 minutes. It will climb five to eight degrees as it sits, and the juices redistribute instead of running out onto the board.

Optional and worth it: while it rests, crank the oven to 500°F (260°C), then return the roast for four or five minutes to blister the surface. A quick blast at the end browns without adding meaningful heat to the middle.

For the gravy, spoon most of the fat out of the pan, mash the vegetables slightly, and stir in flour over medium heat until it smells toasted. Add wine, scrape the pan, reduce until nearly dry, then add stock and simmer until it coats a spoon.
Strain the gravy, finish with vinegar and cold butter off the heat, and carve the roast across the grain in thin slices.
What goes wrong: an oven at 350°F (175°C) and no thermometer. That combination cooks a two inch band of grey meat around a raw core and there is no way to fix it after the fact.
notes: Cuts from the round can be slightly tough even at the right temperature. Slice them thinner and across the grain and they eat like a much more expensive piece of meat.
If the animal was old or hard hunted, braise the roast instead. No oven temperature makes a tough muscle tender in two hours.
storage: Fridge four days. Cold roast sliced paper thin is the best sandwich in this collection. Reheat only in gravy, gently, or not at all.

title: Venison Stroganoff
dek: Sear fast, simmer never, and put the sour cream in off the heat.
intro:
Stroganoff is a fast dish pretending to be a slow one. The meat is cut small and cooked hot for barely a minute, the sauce is built in the same pan while the meat rests on a plate, and the two only meet again at the very end. Anyone who has simmered stroganoff for half an hour has produced something edible, but not this.

Two failure points. Overcooked meat, which turns to grey string. And broken sour cream, which happens the second the pan goes back over heat after it has gone in.

items: 2 lb (900 g) venison backstrap or top round, silverskin removed
3 tbsp beef tallow or neutral oil
1 lb (450 g) cremini mushrooms, thickly sliced
1/2 cup dry white wine or brandy
1 cup sour cream, at room temperature

method: Slice the venison across the grain into strips about a quarter inch thick and two inches long. Half-frozen meat slices far more neatly than fully thawed meat.
Dry the strips hard on paper towels and season them. Wet meat will not sear; it will release water and stew in it, which is the single most common way this dish goes wrong.

Heat the tallow in a large skillet over high until it is smoking faintly. Sear the strips in three or four batches, in a single layer, for well under a minute a side, until browned outside and still pink within. Move them straight to a plate.

Lower the heat to medium-high, add butter and the mushrooms, and leave them alone until they have released their water, it has boiled off, and they are browning properly. Crowded or stirred mushrooms boil and stay pale.
Add the onion and cook until soft and golden at the edges, then the garlic for a minute.
Stir in the flour and tomato paste and cook until the flour smells toasted and the paste has darkened. Deglaze with the wine, scraping the pan, and reduce until nearly dry.
Add stock, mustard, Worcestershire and paprika and simmer until the sauce has thickened enough to coat the back of a spoon and hold a line when you drag a finger through it, roughly 8 minutes.

Take the pan off the heat entirely. Temper the sour cream by stirring a ladle of hot sauce into it first, then stir that back into the pan. Adding cold sour cream straight to a hot pan curdles it into grains and no amount of whisking brings it back.

Return the meat and any juices from the plate, stir once, and let the residual heat warm it through for two minutes. If you are nervous about the meat, whole-muscle venison follows steak rules and reads best at an internal temperature of 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit (54 to 57°C); it does not need the 160°F (71°C) that ground meat does.
Add dill and lemon juice and serve over buttered egg noodles immediately.
notes: Full-fat sour cream survives heat far better than light. Creme fraiche is even more forgiving if you have it.
Leftover roast venison, sliced thin, works here. Add it at the very end and only to warm.
storage: Fridge three days. Reheat gently, below a simmer, or the sour cream splits. It does not freeze well for the same reason.

title: Venison Meatballs
dek: A panade, added fat, and a light hand, which is three ways of saying do not make them dense.
intro:
Lean ground meat makes dense, dry meatballs unless you build in something that holds water. That something is a panade, which is bread soaked in milk mashed to a paste. The starch traps moisture and physically gets between the meat proteins so they cannot tighten into a ball bearing.

Add fat as well, because venison has none, and handle the mix like you are folding rather than kneading. A meatball should give when you press it, not bounce.

items: 3 slices white bread, crusts off, torn
2 cans crushed tomatoes, 28 oz (800 g) each

method: Soak the torn bread in the milk for 10 minutes, then mash it with a fork into a smooth paste. Lumps of soggy bread in a meatball are unpleasant in a way that is hard to describe and easy to notice.

Combine the panade with the venison, pork, eggs, Parmesan, garlic, parsley and seasonings. Mix with your fingertips, lifting and folding, until it is just uniform. Squeezing and kneading builds a springy texture.
Fry a teaspoon of the mix in a small pan until browned through and taste it for salt. Adjust before you roll thirty of them.
Chill the mix 30 minutes so it firms up, then roll balls about an inch and a half across with wet hands. Wet hands are the difference between round meatballs and a mess.
Start the sauce: warm the oil, cook the onion until soft and translucent, add garlic for a minute, then the tomatoes, oregano, sugar and salt. Simmer at a lazy bubble while you brown the meatballs.
Brown the meatballs in a wide skillet in batches, turning them, until they have a dark crust on several sides. They will not be cooked through and should not be; they are going into the sauce.

Slide the browned meatballs into the simmering sauce and cook, covered, at a bare simmer for 25 minutes. The sauce goes into the meatballs and the meat flavours the sauce, which is the entire reason not to finish them in the pan.

Check one. Ground meat, venison and pork alike, is done at an internal temperature of 160°F (71°C), and a probe into the middle of the largest meatball should confirm it. Grinding distributes surface bacteria through the whole mix, so this number applies regardless of species.
Tear the basil in at the end and let the pot sit off the heat 10 minutes before serving.
What goes wrong: too much filler. A panade at this ratio is invisible in the finished meatball. Doubled, it makes bread dumplings with a meat flavour, and people can tell.
notes: Ground pork here is doing the fat job. Ground beef chuck works too; straight venison does not.
These freeze beautifully cooked in their sauce, and they are the reason to make a double batch while the grinder is dirty anyway.
storage: Fridge four days in sauce, freezer three months. Reheat covered, gently, until the sauce bubbles at the edge and the centres are hot.

title: Venison Meatloaf
dek: Free-form on a sheet pan, glazed twice, and never pressed into a loaf tin.
intro:
A loaf tin steams the sides of a meatloaf and leaves it sitting in its own grease, which is why tin-baked meatloaf is pale and slightly boiled at the edges. Shaped free-form on a sheet pan, the whole outside browns, the fat runs off, and there is surface area for a glaze to caramelise on.

Venison needs the same two supports as every other lean ground preparation here: added fat and a panade. Get those right and this is better than the beef version, because the meat itself has more flavour to begin with.
method: Soak the breadcrumbs in the milk and set aside. Melt the butter and cook the onion, celery and carrot until completely soft and sweet, with no crunch left, then add garlic for a minute and let it cool.
Raw onion in a meatloaf never fully cooks and gives you hard hot bites. The five minutes this step costs is worth it.
Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C) and line a sheet pan with parchment.

Combine the soaked crumbs, cooled vegetables, both meats, eggs, Worcestershire and seasonings. Mix with your hands, lifting and turning, only until it is uniform. Overworked meatloaf is springy and dense.
Fry a small patty, taste it, and adjust the salt. It is the last chance you get.
Shape the mix into a free-form loaf on the pan, roughly nine inches long and four wide, with the top gently domed. Smooth the surface so there are no cracks for fat to pool in.
Whisk the glaze ingredients and brush a third of it over the loaf.
Bake for about 40 minutes, then brush on another third and continue. Glazing in stages builds layers instead of one thin varnish that burns.

Bake until the outside is deeply browned, the glaze has caught and darkened at the edges, and a probe in the very centre reads an internal temperature of 160°F (71°C). Ground meat of any kind gets that number, and a meatloaf is the definition of ground meat.
Brush the last of the glaze on and rest the loaf on the pan for 15 minutes before slicing. Cut too early and it crumbles apart along the pan.
What goes wrong: not enough fat. Straight venison with no pork produces a loaf that is crumbly and dry no matter how much bread is in it. The pork is structural.
notes: Bacon draped over the top is traditional and works, but it shields the surface from browning. Weave it thin or skip it and rely on the glaze.
Cold meatloaf sandwiches on white bread with more ketchup are the actual reason to make a big one.
storage: Fridge four days, freezer three months, sliced and wrapped in portions. Reheat slices in a covered pan with a splash of stock rather than in a microwave.

title: Pot Pie Filling, Made to Freeze
dek: Build the filling now, put a crust on it some rainy evening later.
yield: About 3 quarts, enough for three 9 inch pies
intro:
A pot pie is two separate projects that people insist on doing on the same night. Split them up. The filling is a braise that improves with a day in the fridge and freezes without complaint, and the pastry takes twenty minutes whenever you feel like it.

The one thing a filling for freezing needs that a filling for tonight does not is to be slightly thicker and slightly under-seasoned, because it will loosen as it thaws and concentrate as it bakes under a lid of pastry.

items: 3 lb (1.4 kg) venison or elk shoulder or neck, in 1 inch cubes
4 tbsp beef tallow or neutral oil
1 lb (450 g) waxy potatoes, in 1/2 inch dice
8 oz (225 g) mushrooms, quartered and browned
4 tbsp butter mashed with 4 tbsp flour

method: Season and flour the meat, then brown it hard in batches in the tallow until each piece has a dark crust and the bottom of the pot is brown and sticky. Crowding the pot steams the meat and you lose the flavour you came for.
Set the meat aside and cook the onion, carrot and celery in the same fat until soft and lightly coloured, then add garlic and tomato paste and stir until the paste darkens to brick.
Deglaze with the wine, scraping the pot clean, and reduce it by half.

Return the meat, add stock, thyme and bay, and hold it at a bare simmer, covered, until a cube crushes easily against the side of the pot with a spoon. Expect two to two and a half hours; a boil at any point strings the meat out.
Add the potatoes and cook until they are tender to a knife tip but not falling apart, about 20 minutes. They finish cooking again inside the pie, so stop a little short.
Brown the mushrooms separately in a dry hot pan until they squeak and then colour, and stir them in. Raw mushrooms added to the pot just release water.

Stir in the butter and flour paste a lump at a time and simmer until the filling thickens enough that a spoon dragged across the bottom leaves a track that closes slowly. It should be noticeably thicker than a stew.
Add the cream, peas, parsley and vinegar off the heat. Taste for salt, and stop a shade under where you want it.
Cool the filling completely, spread in a shallow pan so it drops through the warm range quickly, before it goes anywhere near a freezer. Portion into quart containers.

To use: thaw in the fridge overnight, put it in a pie dish, top with pastry, cut vents, and bake at 400°F (205°C) until the pastry is deep golden and the filling is bubbling up visibly through the vents. A probe into the centre should read an internal temperature of at least 165°F (74°C) so you know the middle is properly hot, not just the edges.
What goes wrong: a thin filling under a crust. It boils up, soaks the pastry from below, and you serve soup with a soggy lid. Thicker than feels right is the correct amount.
notes: This is a braise, which means the meat goes far past any internal temperature threshold in the first hour and then spends two more converting connective tissue. The texture is the test, not the number.
Any tough cut works. Shanks, boned out, make the best version of this in the collection.
storage: Fridge four days, freezer four months in sealed containers with as little headspace as you can manage. Label the container, because everything in a freezer looks like everything else.

title: Venison Tacos, Two Ways
dek: Fast with ground, slow with a shoulder, and both are better than the beef version.
intro:
Venison takes to chile and lime better than beef does, because the meat has a slightly darker, more mineral flavour that acid and heat lift rather than fight. This page gives the weeknight version, with ground meat in a skillet, and the weekend version, with a shoulder braised until it shreds.

The ground one obeys ground-meat rules and gets cooked to a number. The braised one goes so far past any number that the question stops being relevant, which is worth understanding rather than memorising.

items: 4 oz (110 g) bacon or pork fat, finely diced
3 lb (1.4 kg) venison shoulder, in large chunks
3 dried guajillo chiles, stemmed and seeded
2 dried ancho chiles, stemmed and seeded

method: Fast version: render the bacon in a heavy skillet over medium heat until the fat runs. Ground venison has essentially no fat and without this it browns into dry crumbs.
Raise the heat, add the venison, and press it into a flat layer. Leave it undisturbed until the underside has browned properly before you start breaking it up. Constant stirring steams it grey.
Add onion and cook until soft, then garlic and all the dry spices, stirring until they smell toasted and begin to stick to the pan.

Stir in tomato paste, cook it until it darkens, then add the stock and simmer until most of the liquid has gone and the meat is glossy and just moist rather than wet. Confirm with a probe that the meat has reached an internal temperature of 160°F (71°C), which is the standard for any ground meat and not optional here. Finish with lime juice.
Slow version: toast the dried chiles in a dry pan, pressing them flat, until pliable and fragrant but nowhere near blackened. Soak them in hot water 20 minutes.
Blend the soaked chiles with the onion, garlic, cumin, a cup of the stock, the vinegar and salt into a smooth sauce.

Brown the venison chunks hard in a Dutch oven, pour the chile sauce and remaining stock over, and braise covered at 300°F (150°C) until the meat pulls apart under two forks with no resistance at all, about three hours.
Shred the meat, return it to the sauce, and reduce uncovered until the sauce clings to the meat instead of pooling under it.
For the crisp version, spread the shredded meat on a sheet pan and run it under a broiler until the edges char and crisp, then toss it back through the sauce. This is worth the extra five minutes.
Warm the tortillas directly over a flame or in a dry pan until they puff and spot, and hold them in a folded towel.
Build with onion, cilantro, cotija, avocado and lime. Two tortillas per taco if the filling is wet, which it will be.
notes: Elk works identically. Bear and other omnivores do not; they carry a trichinella risk and must be cooked to a much higher internal temperature. Look up the current guidance for the species before you cook anything unfamiliar.
Double the spice mix for the fast version and keep it in a jar. It turns this into a twenty minute dinner.
storage: Both fillings keep four days in the fridge. The braised one freezes for three months in its sauce; the ground one freezes for two and dries out slightly on reheating.

title: Grinding and Packing the Freezer
dek: An afternoon of tedium that determines what the next twelve months taste like.
intro:
Grinding day is not glamorous and it is where most of the flavour of an entire animal is won or lost. Warm meat, dull plates and sloppy wrapping produce a freezer full of packages nobody is excited to open. Cold meat, sharp equipment and tight packages produce burger that tastes like the animal did.

Plan the whole thing before you cut anything. Decide how much goes to grind, what package sizes your household actually cooks, and how much fat you are adding, and then work through it without stopping to think.

items: 1 meat grinder with a coarse and a fine plate
4 large trays that fit in the freezer
1 vacuum sealer or 2 rolls of freezer paper and tape
1 permanent marker that writes on plastic
40 lb (18 kg) trimmed venison or elk destined for grind
8 lb (3.6 kg) beef fat trim or pork fat, at 20 percent by weight

method: Trim first, grind second, and never blur the two. Every scrap of silverskin, sinew and waxy game fat that goes into the hopper either wraps around the auger and stops the machine or ends up as gristle in a burger.
Cut everything into strips that fit the throat of your grinder without forcing. Forcing is what dulls the blade and warms the meat.

Chill hard. Trays of cubed meat go in the freezer until the edges are crunchy, roughly 30 to 45 minutes. Grinder head, auger, blade and plate go in with them. Warm equipment smears fat and smeared fat means greasy, crumbly burger.
Decide the fat ratio before you begin. Ten percent added fat makes a lean grind suitable for chili and sauces; twenty percent makes burger patties that behave. Weigh it rather than guessing.
Grind once through the coarse plate, alternating handfuls of meat and fat so the mix is even without a second pass. For burger, follow with a fine plate; for chili and sausage, coarse is better.

Watch what comes out of the plate. It should be distinct strands. The moment it turns into a paste or starts oozing rather than extruding, stop, clean the blade and plate, and chill everything again. Something is dull or something is warm.
Package in the sizes you actually cook. A pound for a household of two, two pounds for a family, and nothing bigger, because the leftover half of a thawed package is the thing that gets forgotten.

Vacuum seal if you have the machine. If you are wrapping in paper, press the package flat and thin, force every bit of air out, wrap tightly with the shiny side in, and tape all the seams. Flat packages freeze faster, stack better and thaw more evenly.

Label every single package with species, cut and weight. Do not put a date on the paper if you would rather not, but write something that tells you which animal it came from, or you will be defrosting mysteries in the middle of winter.
Freeze in a single layer first, spread out, and only stack once everything is solid. A freezer loaded with a warm stack of packages takes a day to catch up and everything in it suffers.
Wash the grinder immediately and dry the metal parts completely. Carbon steel plates rust overnight and a rusted plate is a ruined plate.

Remember that ground meat has a higher food safety floor than whole muscle. Everything you just made gets cooked until it is browned through with no pink left and a probe reads an internal temperature of 160°F (71°C), because grinding takes the surface of the meat and puts it through the middle.
notes: Freezing does not sterilise meat and it is not a substitute for testing an animal. For anything to do with chronic wasting disease, sampling, or an animal that did not look right, go to ODFW and your current state hunter guide.
A cheap grinder will do one deer a year unhappily. If you are doing an elk, borrow or buy something with a real motor and a number 22 head.
storage: Ground game holds its quality about four months at 0 degrees Fahrenheit (-18°C), whole-muscle cuts about a year, and vacuum-sealed packages roughly double both. It stays safe indefinitely at that temperature; what degrades is how it tastes.

title: What to Do With the Trim
dek: The bag of scraps in the bottom of the fridge is stock, a confit and a pot of ragu.
yield: Varies, roughly 3 quarts of stock plus a pot of ragu
intro:
After an animal is broken down there is a pile of things that are not steaks, not roasts and not clean enough for the grinder: neck scraps, rib meat, the ends of the flank, bones with meat still on them. Most of it gets thrown away, which is a shame, because pound for pound it has more flavour than the backstrap everyone fought over.

Three uses, in the order they make sense. Roast the bones for stock. Braise the ragged meat into a ragu. Render nothing, because game fat is not worth saving no matter how thrifty you feel.

items: 8 lb (3.6 kg) bones, sawn into lengths, with meat scraps attached
3 lb (1.4 kg) ragged trim meat, silverskin removed, chopped
6 oz (170 g) pancetta or bacon, diced

method: Sort the trim into three piles: bones, meat clean enough to eat, and anything blood-shot, hairy or smelling of gut. The third pile goes out. One bad handful will flavour the whole pot and there is no rescuing it.
Roast the bones with the oil at 450°F (230°C), turning once, until they are deeply browned and smell roasted rather than raw. Pale bones make pale stock that tastes like dishwater.
Add the vegetables to the pan for the last twenty minutes, then smear the tomato paste over everything and roast until it darkens.
Move it all to a stockpot, deglaze the roasting pan with the wine and scrape every brown speck in, then cover with cold water by two inches and add the aromatics.

Bring it up slowly and hold it just below a simmer, with the surface trembling and a bubble every few seconds, for six to eight hours. Skim the grey foam for the first half hour. Never boil it, or the stock emulsifies its own fat and comes out cloudy and greasy.
Strain, cool quickly in a shallow pan, and refrigerate. The fat sets on top as a hard disc; lift it off and throw it out, because game fat is waxy and it will taste of the freezer within weeks.
For the ragu, render the pancetta, then brown the chopped trim meat hard in batches until it has real colour. Set it aside.
Cook the diced vegetables in the fat until completely soft and sweet, about 15 minutes, then return the meat, add the wine, and reduce until the pan is nearly dry.
Add tomatoes, stock, bay and salt and simmer, barely covered, for three hours, until the meat has collapsed into threads and the sauce has gone dark and thick enough to hold a line behind a spoon.
Stir in the milk in the last half hour. It sounds strange and it is traditional; it softens the acidity and gives the sauce a rounder texture.
A braise like this passes any internal temperature target within the first hour and keeps going for reasons that have nothing to do with safety, so judge it by whether the meat shreds under a fork.
What goes wrong: keeping trim you should have thrown away. Thrift is a virtue right up to the point where it costs you six hours of cooking and a pot of stock.
notes: Bones freeze indefinitely for practical purposes. Collect them across a season and do one big stock day rather than several small bad ones.
Stock reduced to a syrup and frozen in an ice cube tray takes up almost no room and turns a pan sauce into a good pan sauce.
storage: Stock keeps five days in the fridge and six months frozen. Ragu keeps five days and freezes four months, and it is the single most useful thing in a freezer on a weeknight.

title: Freezer Burn, and How to Avoid It
dek: It is not burning and it is not spoilage. It is your meat evaporating in the dark.
yield: A freezer full of meat that is still worth eating
intro:
Freezer burn is sublimation. Ice on the surface of the meat turns straight to vapour without melting, moves through whatever gap exists in the packaging, and refreezes as frost on the inside of the bag. What it leaves behind is a patch of dehydrated, oxidised meat that is grey-brown, leathery, and tastes stale and slightly of cardboard.

It is not dangerous. Meat held at a proper freezer temperature is safe indefinitely. It is purely a quality problem, and it is entirely preventable with air removal, tight wrapping and a freezer that is not being opened forty times a day.

items: 1 vacuum sealer, or 2 rolls of freezer paper and good tape
1 box of quality freezer bags, not sandwich bags
2 rolls plastic wrap for the inner layer
1 permanent marker that writes on plastic
1 chest freezer, which holds temperature far better than an upright
6 plastic bins for organising by cut
1 inventory list taped to the lid

method: Get the air out. Air is what carries the moisture away, so every technique below is really the same technique. A vacuum sealer does it best; the water displacement method with a zip bag lowered slowly into a sink does it nearly as well for free.

Double wrap if you are not vacuum sealing. Plastic wrap pressed hard against the surface of the meat first, then freezer paper with the coated side in, then tape every seam. Butcher paper alone breathes and is not enough on its own.
Pack flat and thin. A flat package freezes through in a fraction of the time of a lump, which means smaller ice crystals, less cell damage and less liquid lost on thawing.

Keep the freezer at 0 degrees Fahrenheit (-18°C) or below and check it with a thermometer rather than trusting the dial. Every degree warmer speeds up sublimation, and a freezer that cycles wide swings is worse than one that runs slightly warm and steady.

Freeze fast and in small loads. Dumping forty pounds of warm packages into a freezer raises the temperature of everything already in there. Spread new packages out in a single layer, and stack them only once they are solid.
Fill the empty space. A full freezer holds temperature far better than a half-empty one; jugs of water fill the gaps and act as thermal ballast, which also buys you hours during a power cut.

Stop opening it. Every time the door opens, humid room air rushes in, condenses and frosts. A chest freezer in a garage that gets opened once a week will keep meat looking fresh far longer than a kitchen upright that gets browsed.
Rotate. Put new packages at the bottom or the back and pull from the front. An inventory list taped to the lid, updated with a pencil, is worth more than any gadget.

If you find a burned package, do not throw the whole thing out. Trim the grey leathery patches away with a knife while the meat is still partly frozen, which is when they cut most cleanly, and use the rest in a braise or a chili where the loss is least noticeable.

Judge severity honestly. A few small patches is a trim job. A package that is grey throughout, dry to the touch and smells stale when it thaws is not going to taste good in anything, and pretending otherwise wastes the other ingredients.
notes: Ground meat burns faster than whole muscle because there is vastly more surface area. Package it flatter and use it sooner.
Vacuum sealing roughly doubles the useful life of everything. If you shoot an animal most years, it pays for itself in one season.
storage: At 0 degrees Fahrenheit (-18°C): whole-muscle cuts about a year, ground about four months, sausage about three, and roughly double all of those vacuum sealed. Safety is not the limit here; quality is.

title: Thawing Meat Without Ruining It
dek: The counter is not a thawing method. It is a bacteria incubator with a nice view.
totalTime: 20 minutes to 3 days depending on method
intro:
Thawing on the counter is the most common food handling mistake in home kitchens, and it is easy to see why: it is free and it works. The problem is that the outside of a roast sits in the range where bacteria multiply fastest for hours while the middle is still frozen solid, and you cannot cook that away from a whole muscle you are planning to serve pink.

Three methods that work, in order of how much they cost you in planning. There is no fourth one, and the microwave barely counts.

items: 1 tray or sheet pan to catch drips
1 refrigerator running at 40 degrees Fahrenheit (4°C) or below
1 large bowl or a clean sink for the water method
2 zip bags in case a package leaks

method: The fridge method, which is the best one. Move the package to a tray on the bottom shelf and leave it. Figure roughly a day for every five pounds, so a small roast is overnight and a turkey-sized piece of elk is three days. It is slow, it is safe, and the meat loses the least liquid.
Put it on a tray. Packages leak, and raw meat drip on a shelf above vegetables is how a small mistake becomes a bigger one.

The cold water method, when you forgot. Keep the meat sealed in a watertight bag, submerge it fully in cold tap water, and change the water every 30 minutes. A pound takes about an hour. The bag must not leak, or you are washing the meat and the sink at the same time.
Never use warm or hot water. It thaws the surface into exactly the temperature range you are trying to avoid while the core is still solid, and it starts cooking the outer layer into a grey rim.

The straight from frozen method, which is underrated. Ground meat, stew cubes and thin steaks can go into a hot pan or a braise frozen. It takes about half again as long and it works, particularly for anything that was going to be cooked through anyway.
Whatever thaws in cold water or a microwave gets cooked immediately, not put back in the fridge for tomorrow. Both methods leave parts of the meat warm enough that the clock has already started.

Meat thawed properly in the fridge, still cold to the touch, can be refrozen. You will lose some texture to a second round of ice crystals but it is safe. Meat thawed on a counter should not be refrozen.

Cook it to the right number for what it is. Whole-muscle venison and elk follow steak rules at an internal temperature of 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. Anything ground goes to 160°F (71°C) without exception, because grinding puts the surface through the middle.

Judge whether it is fully thawed by pressing the centre. It should give evenly with no hard core. A roast with a frozen middle roasts into a grey shell around a raw centre, which is the other reason to plan ahead.

If a package thawed and you are not sure how long it sat out, the honest answer is that you cannot cook your way back from several warm hours on whole muscle. Use judgement, and when in doubt do not serve it to people who did not get a vote.
notes: Vacuum sealed packages thaw faster in water than paper wrapped ones, because the plastic sits right against the meat and conducts.

Frozen meat that has partly thawed and refrozen shows up as a large ice crystal layer and a stained package. It is a quality problem rather than an automatic safety one, but it is worth knowing what you are looking at.
storage: Thawed raw whole-muscle game keeps three to five days in the fridge, ground meat one to two. Cook or refreeze within that window.

title: Cooking a Cut You Have Never Seen Before
dek: There are only two questions, and the animal answers both of them.
intro:
Sooner or later somebody hands you a package labelled in handwriting you cannot read, or you get a share of an animal you did not butcher, and there is a muscle on the board that does not match anything in a cookbook. The good news is that meat is more predictable than recipes suggest. Everything an animal has is either a muscle that worked hard or one that did not, and that single fact tells you almost everything about how to cook it.

What follows is the decision tree, and it applies to elk, deer, bear, a goat somebody gave you, and cuts of beef you have never bought.

items: 1 sharp knife to look at the grain
2 minutes of thinking before the pan goes on
2 tbsp beef tallow or high smoke point oil

method: Question one: where was it on the animal? Anything from the back, along the spine, or from the inside of the hind leg did comparatively little work and is tender. Anything from the shoulder, neck, shank, flank or the outside of the hind leg worked constantly and is not.

Question two: what does it look like? Hold it up to the light. Fine, close grain with little visible connective tissue means fast and hot. Coarse grain shot through with white sheets and seams means slow and wet. This test works even when you have no idea what the muscle is called.
Press it. A tender muscle feels uniform and yielding. A working muscle feels dense and resistant, and often has a rubbery sheet you can feel through the surface.

Fast route, for tender cuts: trim the silverskin, salt it an hour ahead, get a pan very hot, sear hard on all sides, baste with butter, and pull it at an internal temperature of 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. Whole-muscle game gets the same latitude as beef. Rest it as long as you cooked it.

Slow route, for working cuts: brown it hard first, then cook it covered in liquid at 300°F (150°C) until a fork twists in it with no resistance and it starts to come apart under its own weight. That is three to five hours and it is a texture, not a clock.
If you genuinely cannot tell, cut a small piece off and cook it in a pan. Ninety seconds and a taste settles the question and costs you two ounces of meat.
Test the grain direction before you carve anything. Find the lines of muscle fibre and cut across them, not along them. Slicing with the grain makes a tender cut chewy and a chewy cut inedible.

Never split the difference. The worst outcome for both categories is medium heat for a medium time, which is too long for a tender cut and nowhere near long enough for a tough one. Commit to fast or slow.

Know your exceptions. Flank and skirt style muscles are coarse-grained but thin, and they work fast and hot provided you slice them very thin across the grain afterwards. Anything from an omnivore, bear especially, has a parasite risk that changes the rules entirely and needs a much higher internal temperature; look up the current guidance for that species rather than assuming.

When the animal itself is the unknown, not just the cut, go to the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife and your state hunter guide for anything about disease, testing or handling. Freezing does not make everything safe and no cooking method substitutes for knowing what you have.
notes: Ground anything, from any species, goes to an internal temperature of 160°F (71°C). That rule never has an exception and it does not depend on which muscle it came from.
Write on the package next time. Two words in marker save an argument every winter.
storage: Whatever it turns out to be, the storage rules do not change: thawed raw whole muscle three to five days in the fridge, cooked meat four days, and everything wrapped tight if it goes back in the freezer.
